call: This funding organization is dedicated to catalyzing multidisciplinary scientific teams to synthesize publicly available data to address fundamental questions related to emergence phenomena in the molecular and cellular biosciences. It supports community-scale synthesis and integration of existing molecular and cellular data to: Answer novel questions Solve long-standing puzzles in the molecular and cellular sciences Develop innovative research and analytical strategies Tap diverse new talent Train the future data-savvy workforce A community-scale synthesis project has three defining characteristics. First, it uses only existing publicly available data and often integrates distinct datasets together. It does not generate any new experimental data. Second, the project is beyond the capabilities of most individual research labs and instead requires collaboration between two or more labs. Finally, such a project requires diverse scientific perspectives and expertise to come together, often resulting in novel, deeper, and broader insights. You research should focus on well-defined scientific questions or methodological developments that advance molecular and cellular sciences through synthesis research to acquire insights from a collaborative, transdisciplinary approach. This RFP invites proposals for Working Groups that will: Address Compelling Scientific Questions: Tackle novel and significant research questions in molecular and cellular biology through data synthesis. Stimulate Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration: Bring together researchers from diverse fields. Utilize Publicly Available Data: Leverage existing data sources to develop innovative research and analytical strategies. Require NCEMS Support and Resources: The proposed synthesis project must demonstrate a clear need for NCEMS support that goes beyond the capabilities of a single lab or existing collaboration. Promote Collaborative Partnerships: Assemble teams that reflect a range of scientific expertise, geographic locations, career stages, and institutional research levels. Adhere to Open Science Principles: Commit to making findings, data, and analysis workflows publicly available in accordance with community-created policies on open, team, and reproducible science. Train the Next Generation: Provide training opportunities to trainees (graduate students and postdocs) through collaborative research efforts within the working group.

proposals.proposal_title: Impact of Heat Wave Stress on Cytokinetic Bottlenecks in Cellular Division
proposals.abstract: Plant sessility necessitates adaptive strategies to mitigate the impact of extreme thermal anomalies, such as heat waves, on reproductive success. Seed dispersal serves as a primary mechanism for habitat migration, a process fundamentally dependent on successful cytokinesis during reproductive development. Cytokinesis involves complex cellular coordination, including vesicle trafficking, cell wall biosynthesis, and cytoskeletal dynamics, which exhibit varying degrees of thermal sensitivity across temperate and tropical species. This study investigates the mechanisms underlying cytokinetic robustness by comparing genetic circuit responses in heat-susceptible and heat-hardy plant species. Systematic analysis of publicly available single-cell and whole-organ transcriptomic, translatomic, and proteomic datasets will be conducted to identify critical bottlenecks in these cellular processes. These findings are expected to elucidate the evolutionary strategies of plant adaptation to diverse climates. Ultimately, this research may provide a framework for predicting heat resiliency and inform future experimental characterization of cellular mechanisms governing plant survival under thermal stress.
proposals.full_draft:
Cytokinesis is a fundamental process for plant development, as the majority of global plant biomass originates from this cellular division. Plant cytokinesis proceeds through the formation of a specialized membrane compartment known as the cell plate, which develops between daughter cells and subsequently matures into a cell wall. This transition involves the replacement of callose, the primary polysaccharide within the cell plate lumen, with cellulose. The phragmoplast, a plant-specific polarized secretory module composed of microtubules, actin filaments, vesicles, and associated proteins, facilitates cell plate construction. Because the phragmoplast diameter is typically smaller than the cell width, successful cytokinesis requires phragmoplast expansion. This expansion is driven by microtubule dynamics and necessitates the coordination of membrane trafficking, vesicle fusion, and endocytosis. Phragmoplast expansion occurs in four distinct stages: microtubule overlap establishment, vesicle recruitment, vesicle fusion and remodeling, and microtubule depolymerization. Each stage relies on a complex genetic network of structural proteins, enzymes, and signaling components.

Cytokinesis exhibits significant sensitivity to heat stress. In tobacco tissue culture, exposure to 38°C for two hours induces cytokinetic arrest and abnormal elongation of phragmoplast microtubules, with organization failing to recover even after prolonged return to ambient temperatures. Similarly, meiotic Arabidopsis cells treated at 36–38°C show disrupted chromosome segregation and reduced phragmoplast microtubule density. Conversely, the flowering sea grass *Cymodocea nodosa* maintains cytokinesis despite partial microtubule depolymerization under similar heat stress. These graded responses suggest that diverse plant species possess both shared and distinct mechanisms for cytokinetic resilience.

Comparative studies indicate that heat sensitivity varies across the plant lineage. Arabidopsis is typically compromised at 35°C, whereas maize remains viable at significantly higher temperatures, suggesting that maize cytokinesis may be inherently heat-resilient. Experimental exposure of Arabidopsis seedlings to 38°C results in cell plate disorganization, the formation of cell wall stubs, and the development of aberrantly long phragmoplasts. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching analysis suggests that heat stress suppresses the depolymerization of phragmoplast microtubules in Arabidopsis. In contrast, maize seedlings show no morphological alterations in the phragmoplast or cell wall formation even at 45°C. This resilience aligns with observations that maize yields remain stable during extreme heat events that negatively impact other dryland crops.

Heat stress also influences the transcription and translation of cytokinetic genes. Analysis of circadian-regulated genes reveals that heat treatment alters the abundance of mRNAs and ribosome-binding fractions for key cytokinetic components. For instance, the phragmoplast-localized kinesin HINKEL is downregulated at both the transcriptome and translatome levels, while the midzone-localized formin AtFH8 is specifically upregulated. This upregulation may serve as a mechanism to stabilize microtubule plus-ends under thermal stress. Such findings underscore the complexity of cytokinetic gene regulation and the necessity of integrating transcriptome and translatome data to understand stress responses.

The theory of biological robustness suggests that genetic networks utilize specific robustness alleles rather than a universal master regulator. Consequently, cytokinetic robustness is likely achieved through the modular control and genetic buffering of distinct processes. Identifying cytokinetic bottlenecks requires the construction of protein networks and the comparative analysis of their behavior under normal and stress conditions. Current knowledge gaps persist due to genetic redundancy and the lethality of certain cytokinetic mutants. The long-term objective of this research is to determine the rules governing cytokinetic robustness under heat stress to inform strategies for improving plant resilience.

This project aims to identify cytokinetic bottlenecks—genes whose products become dysfunctional under heat stress—by integrating existing omics data. The first aim involves constructing cytokinetic networks using single-cell transcriptomics from *Arabidopsis thaliana*, *Zea mays*, *Oryza sativa*, *Sorghum bicolor*, and *Nicotiana tabacum*. A standardized pipeline will be employed to reprocess raw data, ensuring statistical consistency across species. The second aim focuses on comparing these omics datasets to identify divergent responses between heat-tolerant and heat-susceptible species, including the identification of specific transcription factors and cis-regulatory elements. The third aim integrates these layers into a multiplex network model to predict molecular features that influence cytokinetic stability. By analyzing these networks, the study expects to define the mechanisms of cytokinetic robustness, providing a foundation for breeding heat-resilient crops and engineering sustainable plant ecosystems. The project will utilize bioinformatics expertise and computational resources to process large-scale datasets, ultimately establishing a theoretical framework for plant cytokinetic responses to environmental stress.

proposals.proposal_title: Elucidation of Genome Structure-Function Relationships in Human Brain Cells
proposals.abstract: Single-cell analysis has significantly advanced the characterization of brain tissue by enabling the examination of gene expression and epigenetic features. Investigating these modalities independently often provides a fragmented perspective on gene regulation and its relationship to transcriptional activity. This project develops a multimodal generative artificial intelligence model designed to integrate diverse single-cell genomics datasets. The framework aims to elucidate the interplay between three-dimensional genomic architecture and gene expression, potentially uncovering the physical principles that govern cell-type-specific programs despite inherent stochasticity. When applied to datasets derived from patients with Alzheimer’s disease, this methodology may identify epigenetic drivers of pathological progression. Consequently, the study is expected to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative processes. By synthesizing disparate data layers, this approach provides a robust analytical foundation for investigating the complex regulatory landscapes that define cellular identity and disease states within the human brain.
proposals.full_draft:
The human brain represents a complex biological system composed of diverse cell types, each defined by distinct functional properties. Investigating the molecular mechanisms that govern this cellular diversity requires a comprehensive understanding of how a shared genetic framework is regulated through epigenetic modifications. Although all brain cells possess an identical genome, their specific identities are established by covalent modifications to histones and DNA, which dictate transcriptional activity. Characterizing these cells necessitates the integration of data regarding DNA accessibility, chromatin spatial organization, and RNA transcription. While single-cell analysis has advanced the understanding of cellular heterogeneity, current methodologies often examine individual modalities in isolation, which limits the ability to infer causal relationships within gene regulatory networks. This project proposes the development of a multimodal generative artificial intelligence model designed to integrate chromatin accessibility, three-dimensional chromatin organization, and gene expression data. By defining genomic states, this model is expected to provide molecular insights into neuronal characteristics and facilitate a mechanistic understanding of genome structure-function relationships. Furthermore, applying this model to single-cell data from Alzheimer’s disease patients may elucidate the molecular determinants driving disease progression.

The primary objective involves constructing a multimodal model that synthesizes chromatin accessibility and three-dimensional organization with gene expression. Inspired by recent advancements in deep learning—specifically models capable of synthesizing complex contextual data—this initiative aims to clarify the functional role of chromatin organization in regulating gene expression under both physiological and pathological conditions. The proposed architecture builds upon the EPCOT framework, which generates transferable embeddings for DNA sequences and chromatin accessibility. This project introduces two significant advancements: a focus on single-cell RNA-seq prediction and the incorporation of structural information from single-cell Hi-C data. The three-dimensional chromatin organization, represented as a contact matrix, will be processed using a Vision Transformer encoder. This encoder transforms structural data into numerical embeddings, which are subsequently integrated into the expression prediction module via cross-attention layers. This approach allows the model to capture a broad range of regulatory mechanisms, including chromatin loops and topologically associating domains.

Parameterizing this model requires a pretraining and fine-tuning strategy to address the limited availability of co-assay data. The single-cell Hi-C encoder will be pretrained using datasets that provide chromatin organization and gene expression information at single-cell resolution across various human brain tissues. A consensus list of cell types will be utilized to learn cell-type-specific features. The proposed model, termed single-cell chromatin organization embedding (scCOE), will employ contrastive learning to align chromatin organization embeddings with gene expression embeddings derived from scGPT, a large language model trained on extensive single-cell RNA-seq data. This alignment is expected to uncover structurally relevant features linked to gene function. Following pretraining, the complete model, designated single-cell gene expression prediction (scGEP), will be fine-tuned using available cell types, assuming that gene regulatory mechanisms are conserved across brain tissues.

To enhance data quality, tensor decomposition will be employed for dimensionality reduction, outlier detection, and the imputation of missing values. This technique facilitates the enrichment of multimodal datasets, ensuring robust model performance. The project will evaluate the hypothesis that variations in genome organization drive changes in gene expression. By utilizing scCOE, the study will associate structural changes with variations in gene expression, providing insight into how chromatin architecture contributes to neuronal diversity. Furthermore, scGEP will quantitatively assess whether chromatin organization is sufficient to predict cell-type-specific expression patterns. Regarding Alzheimer’s disease, the project will compare chromatin conformation between patients and controls to identify disease-relevant architectural disruptions. By predicting gene expression changes, the model may determine whether pathological alterations in microglia result from modifications in chromatin organization, potentially identifying therapeutic targets.

The expected outcomes include the development of two computational tools: scCOE for the interpretation of single-cell genome organization and scGEP for the integration of multimodal data. Scientifically, this research is expected to transform the understanding of brain function and the role of genome organization in gene regulation. The findings will be disseminated through two manuscripts focusing on technological innovation and biological insights, respectively. This interdisciplinary project requires collaboration across bioinformatics, deep learning, and neurobiology to successfully integrate genomics datasets and construct mechanistic models. The support of the NCEMS team is essential for data integration and the provision of the computational resources required for training these complex models. The project requests resources to support a staff scientist with expertise in single-cell genomics and deep learning, alongside the necessary GPU and CPU infrastructure to facilitate model development and validation. Through these efforts, the study aims to establish a framework for understanding the causal links between chromatin architecture and gene expression in the human brain.

proposals.proposal_title: MaiTool: Large Language Model-Powered Bioinformatics Tools for Microbiome Analysis
proposals.abstract: Large language models, including ChatGPT and BioGPT, facilitate scientific literature engagement by extracting insights and summarizing methodologies. While these models assist in identifying microbiome datasets within repositories like MGnify and MG-RAST, they currently lack direct analytical capabilities, necessitating integration with bioinformatics tools. This project introduces MaiTool, a graphical interface designed to combine language model functionality with bioinformatics workflows for microbiome and ancient DNA research. MaiTool is expected to enable literature exploration, facilitate public dataset access via APIs, and perform dynamic analyses with integrated quality control measures. Existing systems, such as BioMedLM and GeneGPT, will be evaluated and fine-tuned for specific microbiome applications. Furthermore, repositories including HMP, IMG/M, and SRA will be assessed to develop seamless data integration pipelines. By addressing queries regarding specific taxa, MaiTool may allow language models to retrieve literature while bioinformatics pipelines analyze and visualize dataset profiles, potentially establishing a standardized framework for AI-driven interdisciplinary research.
proposals.full_draft:
Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT and BioGPT, have significantly altered the methodology by which researchers interact with scientific literature. These systems demonstrate proficiency in interpreting complex queries, thereby facilitating intelligent data retrieval tailored to specific project requirements. For instance, they can extract insights from publications, summarize methodologies, and identify relevant datasets within repositories such as MGnify and MG-RAST. However, the direct analysis of these datasets remains outside the core capabilities of current LLM architectures. Integrating LLMs with established bioinformatics tools offers a potential solution to bridge the gap between natural language understanding and robust computational analysis. This integration is expected to enable on-the-fly analysis of microbiome data while incorporating essential quality control measures to identify potential dataset issues early in the pipeline. By combining the contextual understanding of LLMs with the computational power of bioinformatics, researchers may streamline workflows and ensure efficient access to both published findings and actionable data.

This project aims to develop a graphical interface, designated as MaiTool, to facilitate the exploration of microbiome-related publications, provide seamless access to public data, integrate quality control, and enable dynamic, lightweight analyses. Such a system is intended to empower researchers to make informed decisions, thereby fostering innovation in microbiome research and related fields, including the analysis of ancient DNA sequences. The research team will evaluate various GPT systems, including BioGPT, BioMedLM, and GeneGPT, to determine their effectiveness in extracting insights from scientific literature. Building upon this foundation, the study will identify five to ten key use cases where the integration of bioinformatics tools—focused on quality assurance, data visualization, and lightweight analysis—can enhance the utility of research results. This approach seeks to create a synergistic system that combines the contextual understanding of GPT models with the analytical power of bioinformatics to deliver targeted insights.

The project will also explore the feasibility of enhancing model performance through the development of a custom LLM tailored to microbiome research or the fine-tuning of existing open-source models. This investigation will help determine the optimal balance between leveraging pre-trained models and creating customized solutions for advanced research workflows. Furthermore, the study will evaluate several public repositories, including MGnify, MG-RAST, the Human Microbiome Project, the Microbiome Atlas of Mothers and Infants, the Integrated Microbial Genomes and Microbiomes system, and the Sequence Read Archive. Each repository will be assessed for data accessibility, quality, and relevance to specific research needs. The team will develop software tools that leverage repository APIs to facilitate seamless data integration. For example, a user interested in specific species, such as *Christensenella minuta* or *Methanobrevibacter oralis*, could use the system to identify relevant publications and access taxonomic profiles through automated bioinformatics pipelines.

The implementation of MaiTool will involve a systematic investigation of GPT models and the development of a standalone application using Java, JavaFX, and Gluon to ensure cross-platform compatibility. The project will deliver several key outcomes, including an enhanced GPT model for microbiome and ancient DNA analysis, a unified microbiome data API, and a lightweight bioinformatics framework. Additionally, the project will produce an integrated AI-bioinformatics system and the MaiTool software, while providing insights into the challenges of integrating AI-driven systems with traditional algorithms. This interdisciplinary effort involves expertise in metagenomics, ancient DNA analysis, and molecular epidemiology. The project requires substantial computational resources, including 10–20 TB of storage, 200–500 CPU cores, and 10–30 GPUs, to support model development and optimization. A staff scientist with expertise in LLMs will assist in model optimization and infrastructure management.

The project timeline spans two years. During the first year, the team will evaluate GPT models and microbiome data resources, design the integration framework, and develop APIs for data retrieval. The second year will focus on the deployment of a REST API, the construction of the MaiTool front-end interface, and comprehensive system testing. The final phase will involve the publication of results and the public release of the fully functional system. By bridging AI capabilities with bioinformatics functionality, this project is expected to advance microbiome research through enhanced data accessibility and improved analytical workflows. The proposed system will provide a foundation for future advancements in computational biology by addressing the complexities of interdisciplinary data integration and analysis.

proposals.proposal_title: Synthesis of Gene Expression Data for the Construction of a Bacterial Cell State Atlas
proposals.abstract: Bacterial cells adapt their molecular composition to optimize survival, yet current knowledge of these states remains fragmented due to the difficulty of harmonizing heterogeneous omics datasets. The NCEMS working group will synthesize bacterial gene expression data using machine learning to construct a comprehensive atlas of bacterial cell states. This project will initially examine model Escherichia coli strains before incorporating wild strains from natural environments and diverse bacterial species. Dimensional reduction approaches will be employed to map the organization of cell state space, potentially identifying distinct foci corresponding to specific lifestyles such as biofilm formation or dormancy. The study will further investigate whether gene expression signatures and their evolutionary relationships are conserved across species. Finally, a classifier will be developed to predict population cell state composition from metatranscriptomic data. These open-science resources may facilitate the non-genetic reprogramming of bacteria to mitigate environmental damage and prevent the development of pathogenic lifestyles.
proposals.full_draft:
Bacterial cells modulate gene expression to adapt their physiology to environmental fluctuations, such as the transition from active replication to quiescence during nutrient depletion. Clonal bacterial populations often diversify into distinct phenotypes, including biofilm or planktonic growth, motile or sessile forms, and specialized nitrogen-fixing cells. It remains unclear whether these cells occupy a limited number of discrete gene expression states with abrupt transitions or exist along a continuum of gradually shifting states. Furthermore, the evolutionary conservation of these states across species is poorly understood, and many potential cell states may remain undiscovered due to the limitations of existing laboratory-based datasets. This project aims to test key hypotheses regarding the organization of bacterial gene expression space and to synthesize these findings into a unified atlas of bacterial cell states. The study will determine whether bacterial cells occupy discrete states, whether the growth–quiescence axis is conserved across species, and whether specialized lifestyles evolved through the subfunctionalization of core states. Additionally, the project will investigate whether a comprehensive atlas can enable the prediction of population composition from transcriptomic data.

Thousands of bacterial gene expression datasets are currently available in repositories such as OKgeneExpDB, E. coli Expression 2, Ecomics, PRECISE, COLUMBOS, and iModulonDB. These resources contain tens of thousands of profiles representing diverse environmental conditions, genetic backgrounds, and experimental perturbations. Although many datasets include curated metadata, most existing resources lack the open-access, community-maintained infrastructure necessary for seamless integration and reuse. Previous machine learning applications have attempted to predict bacterial growth rates and identify co-regulated gene modules, yet systematic variation introduced by differing technologies and protocols often confounds these analyses. Consequently, robust harmonization and advanced quality control are required to facilitate meaningful synthesis and discovery.

This study defines bacterial cell states as distinct growth or lifestyle conditions characterized by coordinated shifts in gene expression across multiple genes. While single-cell RNA-seq could theoretically define these states with high precision, current technical challenges limit its application to bacteria. This project will instead integrate existing bulk gene expression datasets, which often capture nearly pure cell states or mixtures of dominant phenotypes. Dimensional reduction and clustering methods will be employed to infer an atlas of bacterial cell states and the relationships between them.

The project will develop the Integrative Gene Expression Synthesis Tool (InGEST), an open-source pipeline designed to harmonize large-scale bacterial gene expression data. This pipeline will process tens of thousands of RNA-seq and microarray datasets using standardized filtering and normalization procedures while correcting for technical variation. InGEST will incorporate advanced quality control functions to detect anomalies such as DNA contamination or inconsistent replicates. The software will be released as a community-maintainable package with comprehensive documentation, tutorials, and containerized deployment options to ensure long-term accessibility.

To delineate distinct cell states, the study will apply unsupervised learning and dimensional reduction techniques commonly utilized in eukaryotic single-cell analysis. Initial efforts will focus on curated Escherichia coli datasets to identify primary attractors corresponding to exponential growth and stationary phase, thereby establishing a foundational growth–quiescence axis. As the InGEST pipeline matures, the analysis will expand to non-laboratory E. coli strains and natural environments, such as the gut, to identify subfunctionalized states. Ortholog mapping tools will be used to establish a consistent feature space across diverse strains. The analysis will eventually encompass more than twenty bacterial species, including model organisms and pathogens, to explore conserved and specialized expression patterns.

Following the construction of the atlas, the project will develop classifiers to estimate the proportions of cells occupying different states within bulk transcriptomic or metatranscriptomic samples. These models will be trained and validated on synthetic mixtures of pure-state datasets and subsequently tested against available single-cell bacterial transcriptomes. Ultimately, these classifiers will be applied to environmental and host-associated microbial communities to predict functional composition and state distribution.

The project will yield a comprehensive Atlas of Bacterial Cell States, providing insights into the structure and evolutionary conservation of gene expression landscapes. Methodological outcomes include the InGEST pipeline, the Atlas as a community resource, and a Bacterial Cell Population Classifier. These tools will enable new analyses of bacterial physiology, evolution, and ecology by integrating unprecedented amounts of data. The project leverages machine learning to synthesize mesoscale data, requiring reproducible pipelines and community infrastructure. NCEMS support is essential for implementing best practices in data management and ensuring that the resulting resources remain open, reusable, and extensible. The computational requirements involve processing thousands of datasets, which will be managed through scalable CPU-based workflows. The project will span two years, with the first year dedicated to E. coli and the second year focused on expanding the atlas to additional species and refining the predictive classifiers. Publications describing the pipeline and the atlas will ensure the long-term visibility and utility of these findings for the broader scientific community.

proposals.proposal_title: Energetic Origins of Connectivity within Protein Interaction Networks
proposals.abstract: Approximately 10% of cellular proteins exhibit marginal folding efficiency, necessitating preferential engagement by chaperones and quality control machinery. Similarly, intrinsically disordered proteins rely on specific binding partners to achieve functional conformations, suggesting that these proteins exhibit distinct interaction biases. This study hypothesizes that emergent scaling properties within protein interaction networks arise from the promiscuous interactions of unstable proteins and the obligate interactions of disordered proteins. Large-scale interactome datasets will be analyzed to evaluate how conformational properties influence network distribution across diverse organisms. Furthermore, the centrality of proteins involved in supramolecular organization will be mapped to identify topological niches associated with liquid-liquid phase separation. Finally, genetic algorithms will be employed to determine how proteome stability constraints limit the evolutionary accessibility of specific network topologies. These investigations are expected to clarify how protein biophysics and binding efficiency shape the architecture and evolutionary trajectories of protein-protein interaction networks.
proposals.full_draft:
Evidence accumulated over the past two decades suggests that protein-protein interaction networks exhibit conserved architectural properties across both prokaryotic and eukaryotic domains. These networks frequently display a scale-free topology, characterized by a power-law distribution where most proteins maintain few interactions, while a limited number of hub proteins facilitate numerous connections. It is proposed that evolutionary selection pressures have favored resilient topologies, allowing metabolic regulation through strategic nodes. High-degree hubs often possess functionally redundant paralogs, which may mitigate the fitness consequences of deleterious mutations. Within these systems, party hubs form continuous interactions within functional complexes, whereas date hubs facilitate transient connections between distinct network modules. Intrinsically disordered regions are prevalent in eukaryotic hubs, potentially introducing specificities that differentiate single-interface from multiple-interface proteins.

The functional role of a protein is strongly influenced by its topological position, often quantified by betweenness centrality. This metric identifies nodes acting as bottlenecks, which may not necessarily possess a high degree of connectivity. Centrality descriptors are generally categorized into neighborhood-based, path-based, and iterative refinement-based metrics. The magnitude of these connections is determined by a protein’s biophysical properties and cellular abundance. Integrating multiscale biophysical and cellular descriptors may reveal how intrinsic protein characteristics dictate network topology and biological function. Although interactome datasets for organisms such as yeast, Arabidopsis, and humans have provided insights into how pathogens target network bottlenecks, the mechanisms by which cells maintain preferred architectures despite continuous protein evolution remain unclear.

Most mutations destabilize protein structures, suggesting that individual proteins tolerate only specific combinations of stabilizing and destabilizing mutations before being removed by selection. This project will develop a physical framework to describe how interaction network properties emerge from the physical characteristics of constituent proteins. It is hypothesized that increased abundance may compensate for low stability or weak binding, while reduced binding affinity might promote promiscuous interactions. Unstable proteins may also engage chaperone interactions that facilitate transitions between functional clusters. Purifying selection is expected to be less stringent for low-degree or redundant high-degree proteins. Such models may clarify how variations in protein stability, binding, and abundance contribute to overall network robustness.

The study will investigate how modular protein clusters maintain connectivity despite genetic drift and whether chaperone hubs act as topological anchors. Research will determine if unstable clients engaging multiple chaperones transition between clusters and if intrinsically disordered proteins remain anchored within specific modules. By repurposing interactome data to model networks across diverse organisms, the project will evaluate the topological context of proteins with divergent biophysical properties. A primary goal is to determine how protein stability biases interaction networks. It is hypothesized that unstable proteins exhibit enhanced connectivity due to their association with the proteostasis network. This will be tested by constructing high-resolution yeast networks and integrating computational stability estimates, validated by proteolysis-based data and proteomic half-life measurements.

Furthermore, the project will survey interactions formed by unstable and intrinsically disordered proteins across divergent networks. It is unknown whether changes in proteostasis composition alter these interactions or if such proteins remain bound to specific chaperones over evolutionary timescales. The hypothesis posits that unstable proteins form more promiscuous chaperone interactions than disordered proteins. By comparing chaperone associations among homologous clients across species, the study will determine if unstable proteins show preferential attachment to chaperone hubs, thereby preserving network scaling. Additionally, the project will examine how marginally stable proteins constrain network topology. Genetic algorithms will simulate evolutionary trajectories, integrating stability, binding efficiency, and abundance with tunable constraints on chaperone hub number.

The Mukhtar group will curate interaction data to build models for yeast, E. coli, and C. elegans, computing multiple centrality measures including degree, betweenness, and PageRank. Node prioritization algorithms will identify influential proteins, while clustering will be performed using MCODE. The study will integrate single-cell and condition-specific data to parameterize context-dependent networks. To determine if structural properties correlate with network clustering, centrality will be compared to predicted stability and disorder features. Stability descriptors will categorize proteins as stable, unstable, or disordered, with enrichment analyses testing for overrepresentation in high-centrality categories.

The Serohijos and Shakhnovich groups will expand integrative models of protein evolution to the proteome scale, incorporating chaperone and disorder effects. The model will include a fitness function linking native folding probability to free energy and chaperone efficiency, alongside an evolutionary algorithm implementing selection. Fitness will depend on protein stabilities, binding affinities, and abundances, satisfying the law of mass action. This framework will allow exploration of how mutations affecting stability or binding influence network connectivity. The expected outcomes include a clearer understanding of how protein stability and disorder shape network architecture. It is anticipated that unstable proteins will display higher degrees and cluster around chaperone hubs, while disordered proteins will maintain consistent positions. These results will establish a biophysical foundation for understanding how protein properties drive network connectivity and robustness. This interdisciplinary collaboration merges computational biophysics, systems biology, and evolutionary modeling to address these fundamental questions. Support from the NCEMS will provide the necessary computational infrastructure and administrative coordination to achieve these milestones.

proposals.proposal_title: Elucidation of Emergent Structural Patterns in Cellular RNA-Protein Interaction Networks
proposals.abstract: Messenger RNA molecules are continuously associated with proteins that regulate essential processes, including processing, localization, translation, and degradation. These messenger ribonucleoprotein complexes (mRNPs) may assemble into higher-order structures that facilitate cellular organization and responses to environmental stimuli. Although these interactions are critical, a comprehensive map of RNA-protein networks at both nano and micro scales remains unavailable. Existing research has produced a large but fragmented collection of datasets that characterize isolated aspects of these interactions. The current absence of integrative analytical tools prevents the synthesis of these data into a coherent, interpretable framework. This project aims to develop computational methods to integrate disparate data types, thereby constructing transcriptome-wide maps of mRNPs and their higher-order cellular interactions. These tools will be applied to investigate unresolved biological questions, such as the functional consequences of synonymous mutations and the cell-type-specific effects of widely expressed RNAs within diverse biological systems.
proposals.full_draft:
Ribonucleic acid (RNA) serves as the primary messenger of genetic information, relaying instructions from DNA to the cellular machinery responsible for protein synthesis. While messenger RNA (mRNA) directs ribosome-mediated protein production, non-coding RNAs perform essential structural, enzymatic, and regulatory roles. For instance, long non-coding RNAs such as NEAT1 facilitate the formation of paraspeckles, which are distinct biomolecular condensates. Despite these diverse functions, RNA molecules rarely exist in isolation within the cellular environment. Instead, they are associated with numerous RNA-binding proteins that recognize specific nucleotide sequences, secondary structures, or the inherent negative charge of the RNA backbone. From the moment of transcription, these RNA-protein complexes, or messenger ribonucleoprotein particles (mRNPs), undergo dynamic structural remodeling, transport, and biochemical processing. Given the complexity of these interactions, the behavior of mRNPs likely emerges from the collective properties of their components rather than the sum of individual parts. This project aims to establish a comprehensive roadmap for understanding the composition of cellular mRNPs and their higher-order interactions by integrating experimental data with advanced computational predictive tools.

The study will integrate publicly available datasets to construct a transcriptome-wide map of mRNPs. Although numerous efforts have systematically mapped mRNA-protein interactions, these datasets often utilize disparate experimental techniques, complicating direct comparison and synthesis. This fragmentation hinders a complete understanding of mRNP architecture. It is hypothesized that a unified, transcriptome-wide map will provide mechanistic insights into biological phenomena, such as the impact of synonymous or non-coding mutations on cellular function and the cell-type specificity of widely expressed RNA mutations. To address this, a computational method will be developed to integrate heterogeneous datasets by identifying linked features—shared metrics or characteristics—that serve as anchors for data normalization. The accuracy of this integration will be assessed using the well-characterized β-actin mRNP as a high-resolution benchmark.

Following the development of this integration framework, a transcriptome-wide mRNP map for K562 cells will be constructed. This process will involve identifying additional protein interaction partners for each mRNP component by utilizing existing protein-protein interaction databases and predictive tools, such as AlphaFold for structured domains and FINCHES for intrinsically disordered regions. Confidence scores will be assigned to each interaction by comparing the results against high-resolution measurements of the β-actin mRNP. Subsequently, the predictive power of this framework will be evaluated by determining whether it can explain the effects of point mutations on RNA abundance and splicing, as well as the consequences of RNA-binding protein depletion. This approach is expected to clarify why mutations in widely expressed RNAs often manifest in cell-type specific outcomes.

Beyond individual mRNPs, the project will investigate the mesoscale interaction networks that govern mRNP localization and the formation of biomolecular condensates. It is postulated that the physicochemical properties of mRNPs encode their spatiotemporal behavior within the cell. Protein interaction networks will be analyzed using clustering algorithms to identify groups based on shared physical properties, such as binding affinities or interaction motifs. These clusters will be validated using mass spectrometry crosslinking and proximity labeling data. Furthermore, the partitioning of mRNPs into biomolecular condensates, such as stress granules and P bodies, will be modeled using residue-resolution molecular dynamics simulations. By incorporating features like sequence composition, charge distribution, and structural disorder, a neural network will be trained to predict the partition coefficients of mRNPs. This model will be validated against existing transcriptome datasets to predict stress granule composition across different cell types, thereby uncovering the molecular rules governing condensate formation.

The outcomes of this project will include open-source tools for integrating disparate data sources to map RNA-protein interactions at both nano-scale and meso-scale levels. The study will produce a comprehensive mRNP database for K562 cells, a framework for predicting the functional consequences of genetic perturbations, and models for assessing mRNP partitioning into biomolecular condensates. This interdisciplinary effort requires expertise in machine learning, molecular biophysics, and bioinformatics, necessitating a collaborative approach across multiple laboratories. The project will leverage NCEMS support for computational infrastructure, including 60 TB of storage, 1.35 million CPU hours for simulations, and specialized staff scientist assistance. Over a two-year period, this research is expected to provide a robust predictive framework for understanding the emergent behaviors of mRNPs, ultimately elucidating the complex regulatory landscape of the transcriptome. Through the integration of diverse data and biophysical modeling, this work will advance the understanding of how mRNP composition dictates cellular function and the formation of higher-order structures.

proposals.proposal_title: The Role of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins in Cellular Adaptation and Homeostasis
proposals.abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDRs) function as critical regulators of environmental sensing by undergoing conformational changes in response to physicochemical fluctuations. Although individual studies suggest their importance, a comprehensive understanding of IDR-driven adaptations across diverse ecosystems remains elusive. The deep sea, defined by extreme temperature, pressure, and salinity, provides a unique model to investigate these mechanisms. Recent shotgun metagenomic datasets offer unprecedented access to the genetic diversity of organisms inhabiting these extreme environments. This project will systematically characterize IDRs as environmental sensors by integrating bioinformatics, molecular simulations, and machine learning. A multidisciplinary approach will be employed to identify sequence-level and functional adaptations across marine taxa. The study is expected to produce a comprehensive map of IDR adaptations, revealing their emergent properties as molecular sensors. These findings may advance fundamental knowledge of stress adaptation and evolutionary biology, while potentially informing the engineering of robust biotechnological systems for extreme conditions.
proposals.full_draft:
Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) represent critical components in environmental sensing due to their capacity to adopt dynamic conformations in response to external stimuli. Unlike structured proteins, IDRs lack fixed three-dimensional architectures, functioning as versatile molecular sensors that adapt to physicochemical fluctuations. While existing literature highlights the role of IDRs in stress adaptation, a systematic understanding of how these regions enable organisms to thrive under extreme conditions remains a significant knowledge gap. The marine environment serves as a natural laboratory for investigating biological adaptation to variable temperature, salinity, and pressure. The Tara Oceans project has provided a vast metagenomic dataset, encompassing millions of sequences from viruses, prokaryotes, and eukaryotes collected across diverse ocean depths. Analyses of this dataset suggest that temperature acts as a primary driver of microbial community structure and gene family diversity. This project will investigate the biophysical properties of individual proteins to determine how they facilitate survival in distinct marine environments. A multidisciplinary approach will be employed, integrating metagenomics, biophysical simulations, and machine learning to link sequence-level features with functional outcomes.

The first objective involves cataloging and annotating IDRs within marine protein sequences while correlating their biophysical properties with environmental parameters. This work will utilize the Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0, which contains approximately 55 million protein sequences linked to standardized environmental metadata. Protein orthologs will be mapped across diverse environments to associate specific features with environmental conditions. Each protein will be annotated with its detection range and linked to metagenome-associated genomes to incorporate genomic context, such as GC content. Structural characterization will be performed using ESMFold and AlphaFold3, with domains identified through an integrative pipeline combining UniProt annotations, the Chainsaw convolutional neural network, and the Metapredict deep learning tool. For disordered regions, sequence-derived features will be extracted using CIDER, while intrinsic biophysical properties will be labeled via ALBATROSS. Given that ALBATROSS is optimized for physiological conditions, additional labels will be derived from molecular dynamics simulations to ensure accuracy under extreme environmental parameters.

The second objective focuses on simulating IDR dynamics to extract key structural features under varying conditions. Because 3D conformations cannot be inferred directly from sequences, coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations will be conducted to capture structural responses to temperature and salinity gradients. This approach utilizes residue-level models to explore long timescales and large molecular systems efficiently. Representative IDRs will be selected from homologous groups, and simulations will be performed using LAMMPS software across multiple environmental states. To analyze the resulting high-dimensional data, advanced deep learning techniques, including graph neural networks and variational autoencoders, will be integrated. These models will disentangle key variation factors and capture invariant structural features, resulting in an ensemble decoder that outputs multi-vector conformational matrices. These matrices will characterize global conformations, pairwise contacts, and secondary structures, providing a comprehensive annotation of IDR biophysical responses.

The third objective aims to elucidate the mechanisms of IDR adaptation and establish a framework for engineering environmentally resilient proteins. Machine learning models will be employed to distill high-dimensional sequence and biophysical data into a low-dimensional latent space, encapsulating compositional biases and environmentally dependent properties. This latent space will facilitate the identification of chemical features that modulate adaptation, allowing for the prediction of evolutionary trajectories. Generative modeling frameworks will be used to simulate IDR adaptation under progressive environmental conditions, enabling the discovery of design rules for novel sequences. These sequences will be validated through computational and experimental testing, providing a foundation for synthetic biology applications.

This research is expected to provide transformative insights into the adaptive mechanisms of IDRs, establishing the first comprehensive database linking biophysical features to environmental contexts. By identifying universal principles of protein plasticity, the project will address critical knowledge gaps and provide tools for engineering adaptable systems. The interdisciplinary nature of this work requires a collaborative approach, combining expertise in metagenomics, biophysics, and machine learning. Support from the National Center for Environmental Molecular Sciences (NCEMS) is requested to manage the computational requirements, including approximately 440,000 molecular dynamics trajectories and 52 TB of data storage. The project will span 24 months, beginning with the construction of the IDR catalog, followed by large-scale simulations, and concluding with the development of predictive models and the public release of datasets and design tools. This systematic investigation will enhance the understanding of protein evolution and provide a robust framework for future biotechnological innovation.

proposals.proposal_title: Multimodal Single-Cell Analytical Frameworks for Cell Lines with Extensive Multi-Omics Data
proposals.abstract: Large-scale consortia have generated extensive multi-omics data for over 2,000 cell lines, yet these datasets remain fragmented and lack a unified framework for cross-modal integration. This project focuses on seven model cell lines to establish a comprehensive benchmarking resource that aligns DNA, RNA, and protein measurements within a consistent biological context. By utilizing homogenous systems, the study minimizes confounding variability typically introduced by donor or cell type heterogeneity. The research will develop computational pipelines to analyze regulatory interactions and cellular resource allocation by integrating bulk and single-cell perturbation datasets, such as loss-of-function screens and Perturb-seq. These multimodal frameworks are expected to facilitate precise alignment across diverse data modalities, including chromatin accessibility. Ultimately, this initiative aims to provide robust tools for investigating complex regulatory mechanisms. The resulting resource may support future community-driven research and enhance the systematic understanding of multi-omics data integration in standardized biological models.

proposals.proposal_title: Integrated Transfer Learning for Mesoscale Organization Principles via Image Data and Biophysical Simulations
proposals.abstract: Mesoscale cellular organization arises from intricate interactions between chemical, structural, and physical components, yet the influence of these structures on cellular properties remains poorly understood. Although extensive image datasets exist, their potential for secondary synthesis remains largely unexploited. This project aims to integrate morphological and physico-chemical measurements from diverse image, in vitro, and in silico sources to elucidate the principles governing mesoscale organization. A computational pipeline utilizing transfer learning and mutual prediction will be developed to analyze relationships between cellular components, facilitating holistic systems-level predictions across both complete and incomplete datasets. The generalizability of this methodology will be evaluated through three increasingly complex systems centered on the nucleus: nucleus-nucleolus, nucleus-centrosome-microtubules, and nucleus-mitochondria-mitochondrial condensates. These investigations are expected to reveal fundamental organizational principles and demonstrate how integrated data analysis may advance the current understanding of complex cellular systems, providing a robust framework for future biological research.
proposals.full_draft:
Understanding mesoscale cellular organization requires a comprehensive investigation into the interplay of physical forces, spatial constraints, and interactions between diverse cellular components. Recent advancements in morphological profiling, spatial proteomics, and generative whole-cell modeling have established a foundation for mapping organizational patterns across molecular and organellar scales. However, achieving a holistic understanding of the drivers of mesoscale organization necessitates the integration of these components with fundamental biophysical principles. This project shifts the focus from traditional gene-centric perspectives to explore how physical principles and geometric constraints dictate cellular architecture. By synthesizing existing cell imaging data, in vitro reconstitution of mesoscale structures, and molecular simulations, this study aims to develop a framework to predict how cellular architectures emerge from the localization, morphology, and interactions of components. This integrative approach is expected to uncover emergent behaviors and previously unidentified features within high-dimensional datasets.

Quantitative comparisons across high-dimensional datasets remain challenging due to inherent differences in data space. While traditional clustering methods require data to reside in a single space, advances in metric geometry, particularly Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distances, enable comparisons across distinct spaces. Recent applications of GW distances have demonstrated utility in aligning single-cell data and comparing biological networks. This project proposes leveraging GW distances to develop transfer learning algorithms for the integration of biological datasets concerning mesoscale structures. This approach addresses critical gaps in cross-space learning, facilitating rigorous integrative analyses of multimodal data. The research will address several key questions: to what extent does mesoscale organization arise from intrinsic physical properties versus component interactions, and what role do these interactions play in determining the properties of cytoskeletal, organelle, and condensate components? Furthermore, the study will investigate whether a transfer learning approach can infer morphological and physical properties from joint, incomplete datasets.

The proposed computational framework integrates multicomponent image data to predict unseen properties. High-dimensional morphological feature sets describing component size, shape, number, position, and inter-component interactions will be extracted. For live-cell data, dynamic metrics such as positional and shape changes will be included. Dimensional reduction will generate interpretable feature spaces, which may be tuned for exploratory or hypothesis-driven studies, including the dissection of cross-component interdependencies and contextual comparisons across drug treatments, disease states, and cell types. Feature spaces will be sampled along statistical dimensions to reveal feature covariance and specific evolutions. Using GW distance analysis, the study will quantitatively describe feature covariance and predictive relationships between components. This two-step approach involves integrating data across cells by aligning multicomponent images via GW distances to generate pairwise similarity matrices, followed by deep learning on these matrices to reveal predictive relationships. Generative adversarial networks and transfer learning algorithms will facilitate inference, with validation performed using open-source datasets.

To address the complexity of cellular data, the project will incorporate data from minimal systems to compare intrinsic properties in isolated components versus cellular contexts. Morphological and physical feature spaces extracted from in vitro and in silico data will be compared with cell image features. New simulations will be developed to determine whether inter-component interactions account for discrepancies between minimal system and cellular feature distributions. If gaps persist, this may indicate that additional interactors or environmental factors require incorporation. The workflow will be refined through application to three mesoscale systems: the nucleus and nucleolus, the nucleus-centrosome-microtubule axis, and the mitochondria-nucleoid-nucleus complex. The nucleus will serve as an anchor point across these test cases due to its extensive characterization.

The project will yield a generalizable analytical framework, a computational pipeline leveraging GW distances and transfer learning, and predictive models validated for inferring unseen properties. Integrated datasets combining cell image, in vitro, and in silico sources will provide new biophysical insights into structure-function relationships. By enabling the integration of diverse datasets, this project will facilitate systems-level analyses of cellular organization. The generalizable methods are expected to benefit disciplines ranging from biophysics to computational biology. The research requires expertise in computational image analysis, statistical modeling, and biophysical interpretation. Consequently, a multi-lab collaboration is essential to ensure access to diverse, well-documented datasets and to enhance the robustness of the analyses.

The project aligns with the mission of the National Center for Mesoscale Systems (NCEMS) by producing an open-source, generalizable data integration workflow. Computational demands, particularly for GW distance analyses, necessitate IT support from NCEMS, alongside substantial storage capacity for high-resolution imaging and simulation outputs. The project will utilize TensorFlow and PyTorch for deep learning, with the POT Python library for GW distance computations. An estimated ten thousand GPU hours and fifty terabytes of storage are required. Assistance from IT specialists will be critical for optimizing workflows and managing data transfers. Systematic dataset curation and integration will be supported to address gaps in publicly available resources. A two-year timeline is proposed, with the first six months dedicated to core workflow development for two-component test cases, followed by expansion to three-component systems and broader integration throughout the second year. This systematic approach will provide a robust foundation for future investigations into multiscale cellular organization.

proposals.proposal_title: The Role of Transposable Elements in the Emergence of Genomic Innovation
proposals.abstract: This project investigates the contribution of transposable elements (TEs) to genomic innovation and vertebrate diversification through the generation of functional elements. Although TEs constitute a significant portion of the human genome, their repetitive structure often limits analysis via short-read sequencing technologies. The study employs a two-phase methodology, beginning with the reprocessing of extensive public genomic datasets, including ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, RNA-seq, and Ribo-seq, using repeat-aware pipelines and pangenome assemblies. Subsequently, these data will be synthesized to characterize how TEs facilitate the emergence of transcription factor binding sites, cell-specific enhancers, and novel protein-coding sequences. By integrating multidisciplinary expertise and advanced computational frameworks, this research aims to elucidate the complex relationships between TE insertions and regulatory network evolution. The project is expected to provide a comprehensive public resource of repeat-aware genomic analyses, offering insights into how TE-mediated mechanisms drive phenotypic innovation and the development of emergent regulatory networks across vertebrate species.
proposals.full_draft:
Transposable elements represent mobile genetic sequences capable of inserting into novel genomic locations, a process that frequently results in DNA duplication. Approximately half of the human genome originates from such transposon activity, yet the biological and evolutionary significance of these elements remains a subject of active debate. Once characterized as non-functional, these sequences are now recognized as primary drivers of genomic innovation, as they generate regulatory elements and contribute to evolutionary diversification. For instance, a substantial proportion of primate-specific transcription factor binding sites are derived from transposable elements, suggesting that these sequences play a fundamental role in shaping species-specific gene regulation. However, the repetitive nature of these elements complicates functional characterization through standard sequencing-based assays. High-throughput methods, including ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq, rely on short reads that often map ambiguously to repetitive regions, resulting in multi-mapped reads that are typically discarded by standard analysis pipelines. Consequently, significant portions of the genome remain underexplored in existing studies.

Recent advancements in computational and sequencing technologies now facilitate a more accurate investigation of these repetitive regions. Telomere-to-telomere and pangenome assemblies provide a more complete representation of repetitive DNA, while probabilistic read allocation methods, such as Allo, allow for the recovery of signals from multi-mapped reads. Preliminary analyses indicate that accounting for these reads substantially increases the detection of functional genomic elements associated with transposable elements. This project aims to determine how transposable elements generate novel functional elements that drive phenotypic diversification across vertebrates. The study will reprocess large-scale genomic, transcriptomic, and ribosome profiling datasets using repeat-aware pipelines and integrate these data across modalities, cell types, and species. Key objectives include identifying how transposable elements generate new transcription factor binding sites, how they give rise to cell-type-specific enhancers, and how they contribute to novel transcripts and protein-coding sequences.

The first phase of the project involves reprocessing tens of thousands of publicly available genomic datasets using repeat-aware methodologies. This effort encompasses ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and Ribo-seq data from major consortia, including ENCODE, Roadmap Epigenomics, FAANG, and GTEx. Human and mouse datasets will be aligned to telomere-to-telomere assemblies to ensure maximum genome coverage, while human data will also be aligned to pangenome assemblies to capture population-level structural variation. Reads will be mapped using standard aligners configured to retain multiple mapping locations, followed by probabilistic allocation of multi-mapped reads. Peak calling and quantification will be performed to generate consistent, repeat-aware maps of regulatory activity, transcription, and translation. This phase is expected to produce a comprehensive collection of regulatory and expression datasets that accurately capture activity within repetitive genomic regions.

The second phase focuses on data synthesis to elucidate the role of transposable elements in generating functional innovation. The study will identify transposable element-derived transcription factor binding sites, enhancers, transcripts, and translated sequences by intersecting data with RepeatMasker annotations and evaluating evolutionary conservation. Chromatin states will be annotated using hidden Markov models to classify transposable element-derived regions as promoters, enhancers, or other regulatory states across diverse cell types. Statistical analyses will assess associations between transposable element families, transcription factors, gene expression, and tissue specificity. Furthermore, integrative methods such as tensor decomposition will be applied to identify higher-order dependencies between data modalities, such as linking specific transcription factors with transposable element families that activate enhancer programs. This integrative analysis is expected to reveal how transposable elements collectively reshape regulatory landscapes.

The project will yield a comprehensive, publicly accessible collection of reprocessed datasets and reproducible analysis pipelines for repeat-aware genomics. These resources will enable researchers to investigate previously inaccessible genomic regions and explore the contribution of transposable elements to phenotypic innovation. The study will result in research publications detailing biological discoveries and review papers summarizing best practices for repeat-aware data processing. This project brings together expertise in transposon biology, regulatory genomics, evolutionary biology, and computational data integration, as the scale of data reprocessing exceeds the capacity of any individual laboratory. The scope of this work aligns with the mission of NCEMS by synthesizing large-scale data to uncover mesoscale emergence phenomena, specifically how molecular-level transposable element insertions drive higher-order regulatory networks.

The project requires approximately ten million CPU hours for large-scale data reprocessing, staff scientist support for pipeline execution, and storage for processed datasets. Additional resources will support collaborative meetings, data publication, and personnel exchanges between participating laboratories. The project will span two years, with the first year dedicated to finalizing analysis plans and executing repeat-aware reprocessing across all data modalities. During the second year, integrated analyses will be conducted, and results will be synthesized into collaborative publications and public data resources. By addressing these fundamental questions, the study will illuminate how transposable element insertions give rise to new regulatory networks and biological functions across vertebrate species.

proposals.proposal_title: Exploration of the Crosslinking Mass Spectrometry Landscape for Novel Protein-Protein Interaction Discovery
proposals.abstract: Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) provides high-resolution structural insights into protein complexes within native physiological environments. This technique utilizes chemical crosslinkers to stabilize proximal amino acid residues, which are subsequently identified through enzymatic digestion and peptide sequencing. While initially restricted to purified proteins, recent advancements enable proteome-scale analysis of protein-protein interactions (PPIs) within cellular contexts. This project aims to standardize and integrate publicly available XL-MS datasets from the PRIDE repository to enhance their utility for integrative structural modeling. A comprehensive meta-dataset will be developed to catalogue PPIs across human and model organisms. These findings may be cross-validated against AlphaFold3 structural predictions, offering robust evidence for complex formation compared to existing predictive frameworks. Ultimately, these integrated data will be incorporated into the EBI Complex Portal, ensuring broad accessibility for the scientific community. This systematic approach is expected to facilitate more accurate modeling of complex protein architectures in diverse biological systems.
proposals.full_draft:
Protein function is fundamentally defined by physical interactions, necessitating a comprehensive compendium of protein complexes to understand the proteome. Various proteomics methodologies, including affinity purification mass spectrometry, proximity labeling, co-fractionation, and photoactivated RNA crosslinking, are currently employed to infer pairwise protein-protein interactions. Large-scale initiatives such as BioPlex have generated extensive catalogs of human protein complexes, while the huMAP project integrates these data with co-fractionation and proximity labeling results to construct a global interaction network. Although these approaches have significantly expanded the EBI Complex Portal, they often fail to provide structural resolution or identify specific interaction interfaces. Furthermore, these assays typically require complexes to remain intact during lysis, which may result in the omission of transient interactions.

Crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) offers an orthogonal approach by covalently linking reactive residues on interacting proteins, thereby providing direct evidence of pairwise proximity. While historically limited to purified proteins, advancements in crosslinker chemistry, instrumentation, and search algorithms now facilitate proteome-wide applications. Despite these technical improvements, the reusability of XL-MS data remains constrained by inconsistent metadata, non-standardized reporting formats, and the historical difficulty of estimating false discovery rates in complex samples. This project aims to address these limitations through three primary activities: the standardization and reanalysis of existing PRIDE datasets, the integration of validated interactions into the EBI Complex Portal, and the functional annotation of uncharacterized proteins.

The first phase involves the systematic compilation of biologically significant, large-scale XL-MS datasets from the PRIDE repository. These legacy datasets will be re-annotated using standardized metadata formats and reprocessed with modern search algorithms, such as Scout, to enhance data quality. The resulting standardized submissions will be deposited into a dedicated PRIDE Crosslinking database, ensuring consistent access for the research community. This effort is expected to yield approximately one hundred high-quality, standardized datasets, thereby facilitating broader reuse and compatibility with hybrid modeling frameworks.

The second phase focuses on utilizing these reprocessed data to validate and expand existing protein complex models. A curated subset of datasets from model organisms, including yeast and human cells, will be analyzed to identify inter-protein crosslinks. For human data, these interactions will be compared against huMAP predictions, with structural modeling via AlphaFold used to assess the spatial proximity of crosslinked residues. Verified interactions will be incorporated into the EBI Complex Portal, providing higher evidence levels and structural context for known complexes. Similar validation frameworks will be applied to yeast datasets, and quantitative affinity purification data may be reprocessed to further refine these interaction networks.

The third phase explores the functional roles of uncharacterized proteins by examining their interaction partners within the XL-MS-derived networks. By identifying patterns or network features associated with proteins of known function, this study may generate hypotheses regarding the roles of currently unannotated proteins, potentially identifying them as scaffolds or mediators of specific biological processes. These analyses are expected to provide a foundation for future functional investigations and contribute to the broader understanding of the human proteome.

The project leverages a multidisciplinary team with expertise in mass spectrometry, database engineering, and structural biology. Collaboration between the Fried laboratory and the EBI ensures the technical feasibility of integrating these data into established infrastructure. The proposed fifteen-month timeline is structured to prioritize dataset curation and reprocessing in the initial phase, followed by structural validation and functional analysis. Successful execution requires significant computational resources, including extensive CPU time for reprocessing and numerous AlphaFold simulations. By harmonizing disparate XL-MS data and linking them to structural predictions, this project is expected to provide a valuable resource for the structural biology community, ultimately enhancing the utility of crosslinking data in defining the architecture of protein complexes.

proposals.proposal_title: Intelligent Metadata Compilation for Enhanced Reusability and Discoverability of Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteomics Data
proposals.abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics generates extensive datasets, yet the reuse of this information remains constrained by inconsistent and incomplete metadata. Metadata provides essential context regarding experimental conditions and sample characteristics, which is critical for ensuring data remain findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. This project aims to develop automated workflows for the extraction, harmonization, and integration of metadata into the PRIDE repository. Bioinformatics and natural language processing tools will be utilized to derive metadata directly from raw files and scientific literature. By applying structured data standards and controlled vocabularies, these efforts are expected to enhance dataset transparency and usability. Furthermore, a community-driven machine-learning challenge will be implemented to refine extraction techniques. The resulting automated workflows and improved querying capabilities will facilitate secondary analyses, including large-scale reanalysis and artificial intelligence model training. These developments are expected to provide the scientific community with robust resources for the efficient discovery and utilization of proteomics data.
proposals.full_draft:
The adherence to FAIR principles—findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable—has facilitated the widespread availability of omics data through public repositories. This expansion of data resources offers significant potential to accelerate scientific discovery and promote cross-disciplinary innovation. However, the utility of these datasets is frequently constrained by the absence of comprehensive, standardized metadata. Metadata, encompassing experimental conditions, sample characteristics, and instrument configurations, is essential for converting raw data into robust scientific evidence. Currently, such information is often incomplete, inconsistently structured, or sequestered within unstructured formats like free-form text in publications. These limitations impede automated processing, systematic querying, and the identification of relevant datasets for secondary analysis.

To address these challenges, this project will develop automated methods to extract, refine, and associate high-quality metadata with omics data in public repositories. This initiative is expected to establish a foundation for improved data discoverability and expanded reusability. While metadata enhancement is applicable across all omics fields, the initial focus is directed toward mass spectrometry-based proteomics due to its complex metadata requirements and established annotation frameworks. Specifically, the project will leverage the SDRF-Proteomics format, a structured, tab-delimited standard adapted from transcriptomics by the Proteomics Standards Initiative. Although SDRF-Proteomics improves transparency by defining relationships between samples, assays, and data files, many datasets remain inconsistently annotated.

The study will develop intelligent, automated workflows to systematically gather and associate metadata for proteomics experiments, integrating these data into PRIDE, the largest proteomics repository. These tools will extract technical and biological metadata directly from experimental files, open-access publications, and existing annotations. Extracted metadata will be harmonized using controlled vocabularies and ontology terms, creating an enriched layer accessible for secondary analyses. To ensure accessibility, a user-friendly interface will be implemented within the PRIDE web portal, complemented by an API for metadata-based queries. This infrastructure is expected to enable researchers to identify suitable training datasets for artificial intelligence, facilitate large-scale reanalyses such as differential protein expression profiling, and support the re-interpretation of public data in light of emerging hypotheses.

The project will initially target standard bottom-up discovery proteomics workflows, including data-dependent and data-independent acquisition, label-free and label-based quantitation, and post-translational modification-enriched datasets. Future efforts may expand to specialized approaches such as crosslinking and hydrogen-deuterium exchange proteomics. Metadata retrieval will combine extraction from raw mass spectrometry data with the mining of complementary information from scientific literature. Raw data will be converted to mzML, and essential parameters—such as instrument type, mass tolerances, and digestion enzymes—will be derived using established tools like Param-Medic. Organism identification will be achieved through matching against reference data, while digestion enzymes and modifications will be determined via open modification searching. These components will be integrated into an automated workflow using Nextflow to streamline organization.

For literature-based metadata, critical contextual information, such as biological conditions and case-control groupings, will be gathered using a natural language processing pipeline based on large language models fine-tuned for scientific text mining. To ensure accuracy, these models will perform self-verification and utilize ensemble cross-checking. A machine-learning challenge will be launched to drive innovation in metadata extraction, with winning open-source algorithms integrated into the primary workflows. Tutorial datasets and documentation will be disseminated through ProteomicsML to support data scientists and proteomics practitioners. The approach will be validated using a curated set of public datasets with SDRF metadata as a gold standard, alongside a manually curated private test set.

The project will deliver automated workflows for metadata extraction, a community-driven repository of open-source solutions, and enhanced metadata-based querying capabilities within PRIDE. All outputs will adhere to open-science principles, with code released on GitHub and findings disseminated through open-access publications. This interdisciplinary effort combines expertise in bioinformatics, machine learning, and repository management, exceeding the capacity of any single research group. The project aligns with the mission of NCEMS to leverage public data for large-scale synthesis and develop integrative strategies. NCEMS staff will provide support for metadata curation, community challenge coordination, and workflow integration, while CyVerse computational resources will ensure scalability. The project is planned for a two-year duration, with the first year dedicated to workflow development and the second year focused on evaluation, integration, and retrospective metadata generation for existing PRIDE datasets. Final deliverables will include functional tools and datasets designed to serve as a scalable template for metadata management across broader omics disciplines.
